question: When must the word HEAVY be used with the call sign?

options.text: On initial contact with each ATS unit, by heavy wake category aircraft
Only when ATC asks for the aircraft's wake turbulence category on the first call
On every transmission made by any wide-body aircraft
Only when talking to the tower about departure or landing

explanation: Aircraft in the heavy wake turbulence category include the word HEAVY in the initial call to each ATS unit, so the controller applies the right wake separation.

question: What maximum certificated take-off mass puts an aircraft in the heavy wake turbulence category?

options.text: 7000 kg or more
136 000 kg or more
300 000 kg or more, the size of the largest four-engine aircraft
100 000 kg or more

explanation: Wake turbulence categories are based on maximum certificated take-off mass; heavy is 136 000 kg or more. Medium is between 7000 kg and 136 000 kg, and light is 7000 kg or less.

question: Who may decide that an aircraft should temporarily change its call sign?

options.text: The pilot, whenever two call signs sound alike
The operator, by message to the ATC unit
Either the pilot or ATC, after agreeing on the frequency
ATC, never the pilot

explanation: Only the aeronautical station (ATC) may tell an aircraft to change its call sign temporarily, for example when two similar call signs are on the same frequency. The aircraft cannot do this itself.

question: Why might ATC tell an aircraft to change its call sign temporarily?

options.text: The aircraft has changed its destination after departure
The aircraft's call sign is too long to say quickly
Two aircraft on the frequency have similar-sounding call signs
The aircraft is leaving controlled airspace

explanation: In the interests of safety, ATC may tell an aircraft to change call sign when, for example, two aircraft with similar-sounding call signs are on the same frequency.

question: With the standard pressure setting (1013 hPa) set, what does the altimeter show?

options.text: Height above the runway threshold
True altitude corrected for temperature
Flight level
Altitude above mean sea level

explanation: With the standard pressure setting set, the altimeter reads flight level: height above the 1013 hPa pressure datum, not above sea level.

question: With QNH set, what does the altimeter show?

options.text: Altitude above mean sea level
Flight level
Height above the threshold
Height above the highest obstacle within 5 NM

explanation: With QNH set the altimeter reads altitude above mean sea level for the actual conditions.

question: With QFE set, what does the altimeter show?

options.text: Pressure altitude above the standard datum
Altitude above mean sea level
Flight level
Height, usually above the runway threshold

explanation: With QFE set the altimeter reads height, usually above the runway threshold. Commercial operations now rarely use QFE.

question: When the standard pressure setting is set, what must precede the number when a level is reported?

options.text: The word STANDARD, followed by the pressure setting
The words FLIGHT LEVEL
The word HEIGHT
The word ALTITUDE

explanation: With the standard pressure setting set, the words FLIGHT LEVEL must precede the level.

question: A controller says "Skyway 243, QNH 1003, descend to altitude 3000 ft". What is a correct read-back?

options.text: Roger, 1003, Skyway 243
Descending 3000 ft, Skyway 243
QNH 1003, descend to altitude 3000 ft, Skyway 243
Wilco, Skyway 243, descending now to the altitude given

explanation: Both the altimeter setting and the level must be read back. Leaving out the QNH is a common, dangerous error.

question: An aircraft cannot climb as fast as instructed because of its weight. What does it reply?

options.text: STANDBY
UNABLE DUE WEIGHT
NEGATIVE CLIMB
ROGER, WILL TRY TO CLIMB AS FAST AS THE AIRCRAFT CAN MANAGE

explanation: The pilot replies UNABLE with the reason, for example "Unable due weight, Skyway 243".

question: Which elements of a compulsory position report may never be omitted?

options.text: Call sign, position and time
Call sign, level and the ensuing significant point
Next position and ensuing significant point
Level and next position

explanation: A position report contains call sign, position, time, level, next position and time, and the ensuing significant point. Call sign, position and time may not be omitted; the others may be omitted under certain conditions.

question: How many elements are there in a standard compulsory position report?

options.text: Three
Eight
Four
Six

explanation: The six elements are: call sign, position, time, level, next position and time, and the ensuing significant point.

question: What is the sixth element of a position report?

options.text: The outside air temperature and the wind at the reported level
The fuel remaining
The ETA at destination
The ensuing significant point

explanation: The sixth element is the ensuing significant point, the point after the next position. Elements 4, 5 and 6 may be omitted under certain conditions.

question: When may flights be exempted from compulsory position reports?

options.text: When the pilot is too busy
When progress data is available from other sources, such as radar
When the aircraft is above FL290
When the route has no published significant points along it

explanation: Where adequate flight progress data is available from other sources, such as surveillance radar, flights may be exempted from compulsory position reports.

question: How does a pilot reply to "Skyway 345, omit position reports until the FIR boundary, next report KENIX"?

options.text: Skyway 345, wilco
Roger, Skyway 345
Omitting, Skyway 345
Next report KENIX, FIR boundary omitted, Skyway 345

explanation: The reply to an exemption message is WILCO with the call sign, since the pilot understands and will comply.

question: Which two types of aircraft weather observation may be required?

options.text: Hourly reports throughout and special reports on landing
Routine reports on the ground before departure, and special reports only in the cruise
Routine ones en route and in the climb; special ones in any phase
Only special reports of severe turbulence, made after landing

explanation: Aircraft may be required to make routine observations during the en route and climb-out phases, and special reports during any phase of flight.

question: In which kind of area are aircraft weather reports particularly valuable?

options.text: Over large cities with many weather stations
Over mountains, only below 5000 ft
Near major aerodromes with weather radar
Where ground observations are difficult, such as over oceans

explanation: Aircraft reports are valuable where observations are difficult, such as over the Atlantic, because there are few or no ground stations.

question: Which section of a routine report carries ETA at destination and endurance?

options.text: Section 2, operational information
Section 3, meteorological information
Section 1, position
Section 4, remarks

explanation: Section 1 is position (call sign, position, time, level, next position and ETA), Section 2 is operational information (ETA at destination, endurance) and Section 3 is meteorological information.

question: Which items are in Section 3 of a routine aircraft report?

options.text: ETA at destination and endurance
Air temperature, wind, turbulence, icing and humidity
Call sign, position, time and level
Cloud type, visibility and runway condition

explanation: Section 3 carries the meteorological information: air temperature, wind direction and speed, turbulence, icing and humidity.

question: Which of these conditions requires a special aircraft report?

options.text: Scattered cumulus cloud along the route at the cruising level
Light rain
Severe turbulence
Moderate cross-wind on landing

explanation: Special reports are made for conditions such as severe turbulence, severe icing, volcanic ash, pre-eruption volcanic activity, heavy dust or sand storm, thunderstorm and severe mountain wave.

question: What does a special aircraft report contain?

options.text: Call sign, position, time, level and the special condition
Only the special condition
The full routine report plus fuel remaining
Position, wind and temperature, without the call sign

explanation: A special report has Section 1 (call sign, position, time, level) and Section 2 (the special meteorological condition observed).

question: Which of these is a condition reported in a special aircraft report?

options.text: Light turbulence in clear air near the tropopause
A wind change of 20°
Volcanic ash
Moderate icing in cloud

explanation: Volcanic ash is one of the special conditions, together with severe turbulence, severe icing, pre-eruption activity, heavy dust or sand storms, thunderstorms and severe mountain wave.

question: An IFR flight suffers radio failure but can remain in VMC. What should it do?

options.text: Hold at the next significant point for 20 minutes
Climb to the minimum flight level and continue in IMC to the destination
Continue to destination at the last assigned level
Stay in VMC, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome, report arrival

explanation: An IFR flight in VMC follows the VFR procedure: continue in VMC, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome and report arrival by the most expeditious means.

question: In airspace without radar, how long should an IFR aircraft in IMC with radio failure keep its last assigned speed and level?

options.text: 30 minutes after the failure
20 minutes after a missed compulsory report
7 minutes after setting 7600
Until the expected approach time, regardless of reporting points

explanation: Where radar is not used, the aircraft maintains the last assigned speed and level (or minimum flight level if higher) for 20 minutes after failing to report over a compulsory reporting point, then adjusts level in accordance with the filed flight plan.

question: In airspace where radar is used, how long should an IFR aircraft in IMC with radio failure keep its last speed and level?

options.text: 7 minutes
20 minutes
10 minutes
3 minutes

explanation: Where radar is used for ATC, the aircraft maintains the last assigned speed and level, or minimum flight level if higher, for 7 minutes, then follows the filed flight plan.

question: In radar airspace, from which events is the 7-minute period after radio failure counted?

options.text: Passing the last compulsory reporting point only
Level reached, 7600 set, or report missed, whichever is later
The time of the last two-way contact with ATC, or the time of the last read-back, whichever is earlier
The moment the failure is noticed only

explanation: The 7 minutes run from the time the last assigned level or minimum flight altitude is reached, the transponder is set to 7600, or the aircraft fails to report over a compulsory reporting point, whichever is later.

question: If the minimum flight level is higher than the last assigned level, which does a radio-failure aircraft maintain?

options.text: The flight-planned level
The higher of the two, plus 1000 ft for safety
The last assigned level
The minimum flight level

explanation: The aircraft maintains the last assigned speed and level, or the minimum flight level if higher.

question: A radio-failure aircraft was being radar vectored. What should it do?

options.text: Enter a hold at its present position until radar contact is restored, then rejoin the route
Continue on the last assigned heading until the destination
Rejoin the planned route directly, by the next significant point
Turn back towards the departure aerodrome

explanation: When being vectored, or directed to fly an RNAV offset with no limit, the aircraft proceeds in the most direct manner to rejoin the current flight plan route no later than the next significant point, respecting the minimum flight altitude.

question: Where does a radio-failure aircraft go after rejoining its route?

options.text: To the nearest aerodrome in VMC
To the alternate aerodrome named in the flight plan, at the minimum flight level
To the destination's designated aid or fix, holding if needed
Directly to the runway threshold

explanation: It proceeds along the current flight plan route to the designated aid or fix serving the destination aerodrome and, when required, holds over it until starting descent.

question: When should a radio-failure aircraft start its descent from the destination fix?

options.text: 30 minutes after reaching the fix
When the controller is expected to have cleared other traffic, at the pilot's estimate
Immediately on reaching the fix
At or close to the last acknowledged EAT, or if none, the ETA from the flight plan

explanation: Descent starts at, or as close as possible to, the expected approach time last received and acknowledged; if none, at or close to the ETA resulting from the current flight plan.

question: Within what time should a radio-failure aircraft land, if possible?

options.text: Within 20 minutes after the radio failure occurred
Within 30 minutes of the ETA or last acknowledged EAT
Within 10 minutes after the ETA
Within 60 minutes after the ETA

explanation: After completing a normal instrument approach, the aircraft should land, if possible, within 30 minutes after the ETA or the last acknowledged EAT.

question: What type of approach does a radio-failure IFR aircraft fly at the destination?

options.text: The normal instrument approach for the designated aid or fix
Whatever approach gives the lowest minima at the destination aerodrome
A visual approach only
A radar approach

explanation: The aircraft completes a normal instrument approach procedure as specified for the designated navigation aid or fix.

question: In the SELCAL system, what replaces voice calling of an aircraft?

options.text: A text message sent over a satellite data link
Coded audio tones sent over the radio channel
A recorded voice message replayed on request
A light signal from the ground station to the flight deck via a separate datalink

explanation: SELCAL (selective calling) replaces voice calling with coded tones transmitted to the aircraft over the radiotelephony channel, so crews need not monitor it continuously.

question: Why is SELCAL particularly useful on long oceanic flights?

options.text: The crew need not monitor the noisy HF channel continuously
It replaces the need for position reports
It gives the crew a continuous display of their position on the HF chart
It allows the aircraft to transmit without a radio

explanation: SELCAL means the crew does not have to listen to the channel all the time, which is very useful on long HF flights where the channel is noisy.

question: How many audio tones make up a single SELCAL call?

options.text: Two
Three
Four
Six

explanation: A single selective call consists of a combination of four preselected audio tones.

question: About how long does a SELCAL transmission take?

options.text: About half a second
About 10 seconds
About 30 seconds, including the reply
About 2 seconds

explanation: Transmitting the four tones takes about 2 seconds.

question: What happens in the cockpit when the aircraft's SELCAL code is received?

options.text: A light and/or chime alerts the crew
The call is automatically printed on the flight deck printer
The autopilot changes heading
The HF radio automatically transmits a reply

explanation: Receipt of the assigned code activates a cockpit call system in the form of light and/or chime signals.

question: What should a crew do before relying on SELCAL on an HF route?

options.text: Switch SELCAL on only after leaving VHF coverage, then wait for the first call from the HF station
File the code and make HF contact while still in VHF coverage
Test the system on 121.5 MHz
Request a SELCAL code from the tower on start-up

explanation: The crew includes the SELCAL code in the flight plan and establishes HF communications temporarily while still within VHF coverage, so the HF station has the correct code. A pre-flight SELCAL check should also be made.

question: Why is start-up approval requested at many busy aerodromes?

options.text: Because engines may not be started without a clearance by law
To allow ground crew to plan their breaks
To give the operator time to file the flight plan before engines are started
To avoid wasting fuel through delays on the ground

explanation: Start-up is requested so that aircraft do not start engines and then wait with engines running; in case of a delay an expected start-up time is given.

question: After receiving an airways clearance from the ground controller, what reply confirms a correct read-back?

options.text: THAT IS THE CLEARANCE, YOU MAY GO
AFFIRM
READBACK CORRECT
ROGER

explanation: When the read-back is correct the controller says READBACK CORRECT (or simply CORRECT). An incorrect read-back is corrected with a full repetition of the relevant part.

question: What does a controller mean by "expect further descent when clear of controlled airspace"?

options.text: The pilot may descend at his discretion now
Further descent is planned but not yet cleared
Descent is refused for the rest of the flight
The aircraft is cleared to descend to the minimum safe altitude as soon as it is clear of the airway

explanation: EXPECT gives planning information only; it is not a clearance to descend.

question: On an ILS approach a controller says "turn right heading 180, closing the localiser from the right, report established". What should the pilot report next?

options.text: Localiser established
Outer marker
Turning right heading 180 and descending on the glide path
Glide path captured

explanation: The pilot reads back the heading, then reports LOCALISER ESTABLISHED once on the localiser, after which an approach clearance follows.

question: On an NDB approach with a base turn, which report might the controller request after the aircraft passes the beacon outbound?

options.text: Outer marker
Glide path established
Base turn complete
Runway in sight with the approach lights showing

explanation: On a procedure with a base turn, the controller may ask the pilot to report beacon outbound and then base turn complete.

question: What does an aircraft report on arriving at a holding fix?

options.text: Its fuel remaining
Its expected approach time, as estimated by the pilot
Only its level
The fix, level and that it is entering the hold

explanation: A typical report is "(call sign), (fix), FL45, entering the hold". The controller may then give an expected approach time.
